items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of the criminal appeal system in correcting miscarriages of justice. Support your answer with relevant authority.
items.answer: For: two routes from the magistrates' court; Court of Appeal can quash unsafe convictions; CCRC investigates miscarriages and has referred many cases; double jeopardy reform allows guilty people to be retried (R v Dobson). Against: leave is required and many appeals fail; the Court of Appeal is reluctant to interfere with jury verdicts; the CCRC has limited resources and long delays; the "real possibility" test is restrictive. Conclusion: The system corrects many errors but delays and restrictive tests mean some miscarriages remain.

items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. an appeal on a point of law from the magistrates' court (or Crown Court) to the Divisional Court of the King's Bench Division, based on a written statement of the facts and the law applied. [2]

items.stem: Describe the routes of appeal for a defendant convicted in the Crown Court.
items.answer: Appeal against conviction or sentence to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) with leave; the ground is that the conviction is unsafe; further appeal to the Supreme Court if a point of law of general public importance is certified and permission granted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: CA Criminal Division, leave needed; 1 mark: unsafe ground; 1 mark: Supreme Court route. [3]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which the prosecution can appeal in criminal cases.
items.answer: By case stated from the magistrates' court on a point of law; Attorney-General's reference on a point of law after an acquittal (which does not affect the acquittal); reference of an unduly lenient sentence; retrial for new and compelling evidence (CJA 2003).
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark route, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.answer: Law: from the magistrates' court: appeal to the Crown Court, or case stated to the Divisional Court on a point of law; from the Crown Court: appeal with leave to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division); conviction quashed if unsafe (Criminal Appeal Act 1995); further appeal to the Supreme Court requires a certified point of law of general public importance; the Criminal Cases Review Commission can refer cases after appeals fail. Conclusion: Tariq can appeal with leave to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on the ground that the conviction is unsafe, and possibly to the Supreme Court on a point of law of general public importance.

items.answer: The least serious type of criminal offence, triable only in the magistrates' court, such as common assault and most driving offences.

items.stem: Explain two factors a court considers when deciding whether to grant bail.
items.answer: The nature and seriousness of the offence; the defendant's character, previous convictions and community ties; their record of surrendering to bail in the past; and the strength of the evidence.

items.stem: Explain the difference between retribution and deterrence as aims of sentencing.
items.answer: Retribution (punishment) looks back and punishes the offender because they deserve it, in proportion to the crime; deterrence looks forward and aims to prevent future crime by the offender or by others.
items.markingKey: 1 mark retribution; 1 mark deterrence; 1 mark backward v forward looking. [3]

items.answer: The aims of sentencing under the Sentencing Act 2020. Sentencing Act 2020 s57: punishment, reduction of crime (including deterrence), reform and rehabilitation, protection of the public and reparation.

items.stem: Isla has pleaded guilty to dangerous driving. Isla has several previous convictions for similar offences. The judge is considering the appropriate sentence. Explain which aims of sentencing the judge should consider for Isla. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: Sentencing Act 2020 s57: punishment, reduction of crime (including deterrence), reform and rehabilitation, protection of the public and reparation; aggravating factors (e.g. previous convictions) and mitigating factors (e.g. guilty plea, remorse) are considered; a guilty plea earns a reduction of up to one third. Application: Isla has several previous convictions for similar offences; this points towards rehabilitation, reparation or protection/deterrence as appropriate; the early guilty plea reduces the sentence. Conclusion: The sentence should balance punishment with the aim most relevant to Isla's circumstances, reduced for the guilty plea.

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of arbitration.
